Then a passage about breath and new creation stopped me mid-walk along the bay.", "author": "699e12d16ef041f10a195450", "item-category": "69c092cd5c80cc7ef09d9860", "tabs": [ "69c085ddd46b33b7eed0d1f7", "69c085d28383a3710d83adf6", "69c33aae5e60542e77d08f86", "69c49e25e41167250ba62e6f", "69c49e12beca94b04b361ec1" ], "main-content": "

It was a Tuesday evening, somewhere between the end of the workday and the beginning of whatever comes next. Remy was pulling toward the bay, past the slow fade of light off the Salesforce Tower, and the wind was doing what the bay wind does — moving through everything, unbothered by buildings or schedules or the quiet disasters of ordinary life.

I had been carrying something that week I could not name cleanly. Not grief, exactly. Not failure. More like the accumulated weight of things that hadn't resolved — small rebellions against the person I was trying to be, conversations that had frayed, the long distance between intention and action. You probably know the feeling. It doesn't require a crisis. It just requires being human for long enough.

I had been reading Tom Wright's commentary on John 20 that morning — the passage where Jesus appears to the disciples on the evening of the first day of the week. They were locked in a room. He came through the walls. And then he breathed on them.

Wright points out something I had missed every time I'd read that passage. In both Hebrew and Greek, the same word covers wind, breath, and spirit. So when John writes that Jesus breathed on his disciples, he's doing something more than recording a gesture. He's echoing Genesis — twice.

First echo: Genesis 3, the evening breeze. God walking through the garden in the wind of the day, coming to find Adam after the rebellion. The cool of the evening, the sound of footsteps, and a hiding human.

Second echo: Genesis 2, creation itself. God pressing breath into Adam's nostrils. The first moment of aliveness.

John stacks both of these into a single image. The evening of the new creation's first day. The same breath that made the first human, moving again. Not a second chance at the old life. Something more fundamental — an undoing of the long damage, a re-creation from the inside out.

I stopped walking for a moment near the water. Remy was not interested in theological reflection. But the wind kept moving.

What stopped me was the word undo. Wright uses it plainly: this wind is come to undo the long effects of primal rebellion.

I had been thinking about forgiveness, which is real and matters. But undoing is something else. Forgiveness clears the ledger. Undoing changes the nature of the thing. The disciples weren't just forgiven that evening — they were made into new people. Given the Spirit not as a reward for faithfulness but as the substance of a new kind of life.

That is a different frame for what I was carrying. Not: you've failed again, here is grace to cover it. But: here is the breath that makes new people. Receive it.

I don't know what you are carrying today. Perhaps it has a name, perhaps not. But I wonder if the question is not whether you can resolve it — whether you can try harder, do better, close the gap by force — but whether you are willing to receive a breath that re-makes rather than merely repairs.

The disciples were locked in a room. They didn't go looking for Jesus. He came through the walls to find them. And then he breathed.

Maybe that is still how it works. Not the wind we generate. The wind that moves through locked rooms, unbothered by the walls.
